title: Help everywhere
hook: Guru Gobind Singh, be our help everywhere

segments.voice: Yesterday: the nine treasures, and your line: nine treasures home. Which treasure did you name out loud? Today, the tenth Guru, and the last line of the opening stanza. Day six hundred nineteen.

Here's a small detail that's easy to miss when you hear the Ardas at full speed. The opening stanza was written by Guru Gobind Singh. He names Guru Nanak, and then each Guru after him, one by one, all the way to his own father, Guru Tegh Bahadur. And then he stops. He doesn't name himself. Of course he doesn't: it's his poem. But Sikhs who pray the Ardas today hear the tenth Guru's name right after the ninth, with exactly the same words. Someone added it, and the words they chose had been sitting at the end of the stanza all along. Today: help everywhere.
screen: `THE TENTH GURU WROTE THE STANZA.` → `HE STOPS AT HIS FATHER.` → `SOMEONE ADDED HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: Guru Gobind Singh's stanza ends with the words sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai: be our help in every place. Sabh is all. Thaaeen is places. Sahaai, our old friend, is the helper. So the Var's opening ends by asking all the Gurus it has named to be our help, everywhere. Then the Ardas, as Sikhs pray it, continues: dasvaan paatshaah, sri guru gobind singh sahib ji, sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai. The tenth master, Guru Gobind Singh, be our help in every place. The community took the poem's last line and gave it to the poet. The poet, who left himself out, is written back in. And it fits him. Guru Gobind Singh's life covered nearly every kind of place a person can be. He became Guru as a boy after his father's execution. He wrote poetry and, tradition says, kept a court of poets at Anandpur. He founded the Khalsa. He fought battles, lost his sons, and lived through siege, flight and grief. And before his death, Sikh tradition says, he ended the line of human Gurus and told the Sikhs that the Guru from then on would be the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, with the Khalsa community. So be our help everywhere isn't a vague wish. It's asked of someone remembered in the court and on the battlefield, in the forest and in grief. Sikhs ask him to be present in every place they go: the job interview, the hospital waiting room, the long drive home. Notice, too, that the prayer doesn't ask for help in some places. Sabh thaaeen. All of them.
screen: `SABH THAAEEN: IN EVERY PLACE.` · `THE POEM'S LINE, GIVEN TO THE POET.` · `A LIFE THAT WENT EVERYWHERE.` · `ALL PLACES, NOT SOME.` · then, large: `HELP EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for help in one place. Sit and breathe. Think through the places you'll be today or this week: your desk, your car, a hard conversation, a waiting room, your own kitchen late at night. Pick the one where you feel most alone. Picture yourself there. If you pray, you can ask, in the Ardas's own words, sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai, be our help in every place, and feel that it includes this one. If you don't, picture someone you trust standing beside you there. The bell holds the time.
Help everywhere. Sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai: the last line of the tenth Guru's stanza, which the Ardas gives back to him.
Your line: help everywhere. When you arrive at the place you pictured, pause at the door for one breath and say the line. Day six hundred nineteen.

screen: `DAY 619 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LIGHT OF THE TEN.`

howItsDone: After remembering the first nine Gurus in Guru Gobind Singh's own stanza, the Ardas names the tenth master, Guru Gobind Singh, and asks him to be the community's help in every place.

he stopped at his father; the Ardas adds his name with the same words.

not some places: all of them.

fork.setup: you're praying the Ardas. the stanza has named nine Gurus and ended: be our help in every place. what comes next?
options: the tenth master is named, with the same words: be our help in every place.
the names start again from Guru Nanak.
fork.reveal: the community took the poem's last line and gave it to the poet, Guru Gobind Singh.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sabh thaaeen, in every place; the refrain that closes the Ardas's opening stanza.

trapdoor: what you thought: help everywhere is a general blessing.
what it means: it's the stanza's last line, given back to the tenth Guru, asking for help in every single place.
what a scholar hears: the Var's first pauri ends sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai after Guru Tegh Bahadur; the line naming Guru Gobind Singh is a later addition by the Panth.
